content: The integration of palliative care into healthcare systems, particularly pediatric palliative care (PPC), is essential for addressing the needs of patients with serious or life-threatening conditions. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), such conditions are often diagnosed at secondary or tertiary hospitals, where palliative care and symptom management are typically initiated. Therefore, it is critical that palliative care services are accessible at these institutions to provide initial symptom control, maintain symptom relief during treatment, and develop a plan for ensuring patient comfort after discharge to a lower-level facility or home. When treatment at secondary or tertiary hospitals is unnecessary or inappropriate, and when the patient’s symptoms are not complex or refractory, palliative care can be initiated at a first-level hospital, with home care plans established. In most cases, follow-up care can be provided by home care services based at the patient’s local community health center (CHC) after symptoms have been controlled and a palliative care plan has been developed at a higher level of care. In rare cases of severe, refractory suffering, patients may require end-of-life inpatient care at a first-, second-, or third-level hospital. Examples include non-viable premature neonates with respiratory failure or patients with severe, refractory pain due to end-stage cancer. For patients whose symptoms are well-controlled but whose families are unable to provide adequate care at home, CHCs should offer inpatient end-of-life care for a limited number of patients at a time. However, in most cases, patients should be able to remain at home with follow-up surveillance by community health workers (CHWs) and additional care provided as needed at home, the CHC, or the palliative care outpatient clinic of the district (first-level) hospital. National healthcare policies must clearly define the types of palliative care services to be implemented at each level of the healthcare system and specify the training required for palliative care providers at each level. Palliative care interventions should be delivered through various platforms, including mobile outreach/home care, CHCs, first-level hospitals, and secondand third-level hospitals. For patients with well-controlled symptoms related to serious or life-limiting health problems, CHWs can provide surveillance and emotional support, with visits from nurses, doctors, or social workers as needed. Outpatient care and home visits may also be provided by nurses and doctors with basic palliative care training. Inpatient hospice care may be necessary in cases where families cannot provide adequate care at home, and no inpatient care is available at CHCs. Small palliative care teams, including part-time doctors with basic or intermediate training in palliative care, can provide outpatient and inpatient care. Ideally, a palliative care specialist physician should lead the team at major cancer centers and general hospitals. Inpatient palliative care wards and outpatient clinics should be available at higher-level hospitals, staffed by clinicians with advanced training in palliative care. Effective communication between palliative care providers at all levels of the healthcare system is crucial. For example, CHWs must be able to quickly contact nurses or supervisors at CHCs, and CHC providers must be able to reach district-level supervisors for advice on complicated cases. Providers at third-level hospitals must also be able to communicate with CHCs to provide information about patients being discharged for home palliative care. Mobile phones are typically used for this communication, as texting is often inadequate for conveying important clinical information. In LMICs with underdeveloped referral systems, standardized palliative care handover forms should be used to document the patient’s clinical and social history, including disease-modifying and palliative treatments, key family members and caregivers, and agreed-upon goals of care. Budgets for palliative care should include funding for telecommunications, printing of such forms, and transportation for CHC staff to visit patients at home as needed. Palliative care training at all levels should be integrated into the healthcare education system in each country or region. This includes basic training for all healthcare workers, intermediate training for those routinely working with patients with life-threatening illnesses, and specialist training for managing complex palliative care needs. Basic training, lasting approximately 35 hours, should be included in the curricula of medical and nursing schools and provided to all primary care clinicians. Intermediate training, lasting approximately 70 hours, should be integrated into specialist training programs for healthcare workers in fields such as oncology, infectious diseases, pediatrics, geriatrics, and internal medicine. Specialist palliative care training should prepare healthcare professionals to manage integrated care for patients with complex needs. This training should include both classroom and bedside teaching and may be offered as a discrete course or integrated into other courses throughout the curriculum. For example, training on pain management can be included in courses on the nervous system, and training on patient-clinician communication can be included in courses on psychiatry or medical ethics. The establishment of university-based palliative care departments or training centers is encouraged to support education, research, and technical assistance for policy writing and clinical service implementation. These centers can also advocate for the integration of palliative care into generalist services, ensuring that basic palliative care is accessible to all in need and that specialist care is reserved for those with the greatest complexity of needs.
